concepts.title: Protein in everyday food
concepts.hook: India's food guide (ICMR-NIN) says cereals and pulses fill gaps in each other's protein, which is why dal and rice work well together.
concepts.rule: Protein is built from amino acids, and nine of them have to come from food. Cereals and pulses fill each other's gaps. India's guide sets 0.83 g of protein per kg of body weight a day.

claims.text: Pulses are protein-rich plant foods.
Cereals or millets and pulses can fill gaps in each other’s amino acid mix.
The body uses 20 amino acids to build proteins. Nine of them cannot be made in the body, so they come from food.
India's food guide sets a daily protein allowance of 0.83 g per kg of body weight, about 54 g for a 65 kg adult.
India's food guide says cereals and pulses in a 3 to 1 ratio by raw weight meet the need for all essential amino acids.
Protein gives 4 kcal of energy per gram, and fat gives 9 kcal per gram.

items.stem: At the school canteen, a student eats only plain rice for lunch. Which amino acid is likely to run short?

options.feedback: Cereals like rice are low in lysine. A pulse such as dal would bring it in.
Rice has a fair amount of methionine. It is pulses that run low on it.

options.text: None; rice has every one in plenty.
options.feedback: Rice is low in lysine, which is why India pairs it with dal.

items.stem: In a hostel mess, the cook has 300 g of raw rice. About how much raw dal keeps the guide's 3 to 1 ratio?

options.feedback: Three parts rice to one part dal means 300 g of rice needs about 100 g of dal.
Equal amounts would be 1 to 1. The guide uses three times more cereal than pulse.
That flips the ratio. The cereal is the larger part, so the dal is a third of 300 g.

items.stem: Using the guide's 0.83 g of protein per kg, estimate the daily figure for a 60 kg adult.

options.feedback: Multiply 60 by 0.83 to get about 50 g of protein a day.
That treats 0.83 as a total. It is per kg, so multiply it by 60.
The decimal slipped. 60 times 0.83 is about 50, not 600.

items.stem: Which of these foods does India's food guide list as a rich source of protein?

options.feedback: They are a pulse, and the guide names pulses as rich in protein.
They fill you up, but they are mostly starch with little protein.
These are mostly water. Pulses like chickpeas bring far more protein.

items.stem: Why does an adult who has stopped growing still need protein from food?

options.text: Body tissues break down and need replacing.
options.feedback: The guide says protein is needed to replace tissues that are broken down, not only for growth.

options.text: Protein is only for growing children.
options.feedback: Children need it to grow, but adults also need it for repair and to make enzymes.

options.text: Protein is needed only on gym days.
options.feedback: The body uses protein every day, to repair tissue and make enzymes and hormones.

items.stem: Amino acids that the body cannot make, and so has to get from food, are called ___ amino acids.

options.feedback: They are called essential because food is the only way to get them.
That name is for the 11 amino acids the body can make by itself.
There is no such group. The ones the body cannot make are called essential.

items.stem: A poster says most Indian adults eat far too little protein to reach the daily figure. What does the guide say?

options.text: A usual adult diet gives 60 to 70 g, above the need.
options.feedback: The guide says the amount is often enough. The mix of amino acids is the bigger worry.

options.text: Most diets give under 20 g a day.
options.feedback: The guide gives a far higher figure, about 60 to 70 g in a usual adult diet.

options.text: Only meat eaters reach the figure.
options.feedback: Plant diets can meet the amount too. Cereals with pulses also fix the amino acid mix.

items.stem: Match each nutrient to the energy it gives per gram.

options.feedback: It gives about 4 kcal for every gram, the same as carbohydrate.
This is the energy from one gram of protein or carbohydrate.
It is the most energy-dense nutrient, giving about 9 kcal per gram.
This is the energy from one gram of fat or oil.

misconceptions.correction: Pulses are a substantial plant source of protein.

misconceptions.name: One meal needs a perfect protein
misconceptions.correction: A varied diet can draw amino acids from different foods.

misconceptions.name: Everyone eats too little protein
misconceptions.correction: India's guide says a usual adult diet often gives 60 to 70 g, more than the need.

steps.title: Protein is built from amino acids

hook.stem: How many of the body's 20 amino acids have to come from food?

options.feedback: Right. The body makes the other 11, but nine have to come from what we eat.
The body can make 11 of them itself. Only nine have to come from food.

options.text: None; the body makes them all.
options.feedback: Nine cannot be made in the body, so food has to supply them.

steps.teach: Proteins are chains of amino acids. The body uses 20 kinds. It can make 11, but nine have to come from food, so they are called essential.

example.ask: Tap the part that has to come from food.
parts: Riya's body uses 20 amino acids to build proteins,
it can make 11 of them itself,
and the other nine come from her dal, milk and rice.
example.spot: and the other nine come from her dal, milk and rice.
example.feedback: The nine essential amino acids cannot be made in the body, so her food supplies them.

guided.stem: Why do we call nine of the amino acids essential?
guided.hint: Think about where the body gets them.

options.feedback: Yes. Since the body cannot make them, they have to come from food.
Size is not the reason. They are essential because the body cannot make them.
Plant foods have them too, especially when cereals and pulses are eaten together.

guided.stem: Which of these does protein help the body make?
guided.hint: India's food guide lists enzymes, hormones and haemoglobin.

options.feedback: Right. Proteins make enzymes, hormones and haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.
Protein does far more than that. It builds enzymes, hormones and haemoglobin.
Protein gives some energy, but its main jobs are building and repair.

steps.takeaway: Nine of the 20 amino acids have to come from food.

steps.title: Cereal and pulse fill each other's gaps

hook.stem: Rice is low in one amino acid that dal has plenty of. What does eating them together do?

options.feedback: Right. Rice brings what dal is low in, and dal brings what rice is low in.
Nothing cancels. The two foods add to each other and give better protein.
Proteins differ in their amino acids, which is why the pair works better than one alone.

steps.teach: Cereals are low in an amino acid called lysine. Pulses have plenty of it. Pulses are low in one that cereals have, so together they fill both gaps.

example.ask: Tap why the pair works.
parts: At the hostel mess, Arjun eats rice
with a bowl of rajma,
so the beans cover the amino acid the rice is low in.
example.spot: so the beans cover the amino acid the rice is low in.
example.feedback: Rajma is a pulse rich in lysine, the amino acid that rice is short of.

guided.stem: Roti is low in lysine. Which side dish brings the most lysine?

options.feedback: Yes. Chana dal is a pulse, and pulses are rich in lysine.
More roti adds more of the same mix. It is still low in lysine.
Tea gives almost no protein, so it cannot fill the gap.

guided.stem: By raw weight, India's food guide pairs cereal and pulse in what ratio?

options.text: Three parts cereal to one part pulse.
options.feedback: Right. The guide gives 3 to 1, cereal to pulse, by raw weight.

options.text: One part cereal to three parts pulse.
options.feedback: That flips it. The guide puts cereal as the larger part, at 3 to 1.
The guide uses more cereal than pulse, in a 3 to 1 ratio.

steps.takeaway: Cereal plus pulse covers the amino acids each one lacks.

steps.title: How much protein a day

hook.stem: About how much protein a day does India's food guide set for a 65 kg adult?

options.feedback: Right. At 0.83 g for each kg of body weight, 65 kg comes to about 54 g.
That is far too high. The guide works out to about 54 g for 65 kg.
That is far too low. The guide works out to about 54 g for 65 kg.

steps.teach: India's guide sets 0.83 g of protein for each kg of body weight a day. For a 65 kg adult, that comes to about 54 g.

guided.stem: Using 0.83 g per kg, what is the guide figure for an 80 kg adult?

options.feedback: Yes. 80 times 0.83 is about 66 g a day.
That uses 1 g per kg. At 0.83 g per kg it is about 66 g.
The decimal slipped. 80 times 0.83 is about 66, not 830.

guided.stem: How much energy does one gram of protein give?
guided.hint: Protein and carbohydrate give the same per gram.

options.feedback: Right. Protein gives 4 kcal per gram, the same as carbohydrate.
That is the figure for fat. Protein gives 4 kcal per gram.
Protein does give energy, about 4 kcal for each gram.

steps.takeaway: The guide sets 0.83 g of protein per kg each day.

concepts.title: Free sugars
concepts.hook: WHO counts the sugar in fruit juice as free sugar, even when no spoonful of sugar was added.
concepts.rule: WHO free sugars include added sugar, honey, syrups and fruit juice sugars. On a 2,000-kcal day, below 10% of energy is about 50 g; 5% or less may add benefit.

claims.text: WHO counts added sugar and the sugars in honey, syrups and fruit juice as free sugars, but not the sugars in whole fresh fruit, vegetables or milk.
WHO says free sugars should give less than 10% of daily energy. At 5% or less, there may be more benefit.
On a 2,000 kcal day, 10% of energy from free sugars is about 50 g, or about 12 level teaspoons.
One can of sugar-sweetened soda can hold up to 40 g of free sugars, about 10 teaspoons.
India's food guide says sugar should give less than 5% of daily energy for adults.

items.stem: At the college canteen, Riya swaps her soft drink for a 'no added sugar' fruit juice. Will her drink still have free sugar?

options.feedback: WHO counts the sugars in fruit juice as free sugars, even when no sugar is added.
The label is right that nothing was added, but WHO still counts juice sugars.

options.text: Only if the juice came from a packet.
options.feedback: Fresh or packed, juice sugars count as free sugars by WHO.

items.stem: During exam week, Om drinks two cans of cola a day. Up to how much free sugar could that be?

options.feedback: Each can can hold up to 40 g, so two cans can reach about 80 g.
A single can can hold up to 40 g, so two cans hold far more than 8 g.
That is the figure for one can. Two cans double it to about 80 g.

items.stem: Estimate how much free sugar fits under the stricter 5% level on a 2,000 kcal day.

options.feedback: WHO gives roughly 25 g, or 6 teaspoons, for the 5% level. India’s guide also uses 5% for adults.
That is twice the 10% limit. The 5% level is half of 50 g.
That reads 5% as 5 grams. 5% of 2,000 kcal is about 25 g of sugar.

items.stem: Which of these adds free sugar to a meal?

options.feedback: WHO names syrups in its list, so syrup on pancakes counts as free sugar.
Sugar inside whole fresh fruit is not counted as free sugar.
The sugar inside fresh vegetables is left out of the free sugar count.

items.stem: Why did WHO set a limit on free sugars at all?

options.text: More sugar is linked to tooth decay and weight gain.
options.feedback: WHO based its limit on evidence about tooth decay and body weight.

options.text: Sugar has no energy in it.
options.feedback: Sugar does give energy. The limit comes from its links to tooth decay and weight.

options.text: Sugar stops the body using protein.
options.feedback: That was not the reason. WHO pointed to tooth decay and weight gain.

items.stem: Sugars added to food, plus the sugars in honey, syrups and juice, are called ___ sugars.

options.feedback: WHO calls them free sugars, and its limit applies to all of them.
Honey is natural, yet it still counts. WHO uses the term free sugars.
Sugars held inside whole fruit are the ones left out. The term is free sugars.

items.stem: A friend says the sugar limit is exactly 50 g for everyone, however much they eat. What is not quite right?

options.text: The limit is 10% of energy, so the grams change.
options.feedback: WHO gives 50 g for a person eating about 2,000 kcal. Eating more or less shifts the grams.

options.text: Nothing; 50 g is the same for all.
options.feedback: The 50 g figure is for a 2,000 kcal day. The rule itself is 10% of energy.
WHO set the limit for adults and children alike.

items.stem: Match each food to WHO's free sugar figure for it.

options.feedback: A single can can hold up to 40 g, around 10 teaspoons.
This is how much free sugar one can of soda can hold.
A spoonful of this sauce holds about 4 g, around one teaspoon.
This is the free sugar in one tablespoon of ketchup.

misconceptions.name: Natural sweeteners are exempt
misconceptions.correction: Honey and juice sugars count as free sugars.

misconceptions.name: All fruit sugar is free sugar
misconceptions.correction: The guidance treats whole fruit differently from juice.

misconceptions.name: Skipping sweets means little sugar

steps.title: What counts as free sugar

hook.stem: Which sugar does WHO count as free sugar?

options.text: Sugar in a glass of orange juice.
options.feedback: Right. Juice sugars count as free sugars, even with nothing added.
Sugar still inside whole fresh fruit is not counted as free sugar.
WHO leaves out the sugar that is naturally in milk.

steps.teach: Free sugars are sugars added by a cook, a factory or you. Sugars in honey, syrups and fruit juice count too. Whole fruit and milk do not.

example.ask: Tap the free sugar.
parts: For breakfast, Kabir has a banana,
a glass of plain milk,
and a spoon of honey on his toast.
example.spot: and a spoon of honey on his toast.
example.feedback: Honey counts as free sugar. The sugar inside the whole banana and plain milk does not.

guided.stem: Fresh mango is blended into juice. By WHO, what happens to its sugar?
guided.hint: Juice is named in WHO's list.

options.text: It now counts as free sugar.
options.feedback: Yes. Once fruit becomes juice, its sugars count as free sugars.
Juice is on the list, so blended mango sugar now counts.
Blending does not change sugar into protein. It frees the sugar into juice.

guided.stem: Jaggery is stirred into a sweet. Does it count as free sugar?

options.feedback: Right. Any sugar added by a cook counts, whatever its colour or source.
Being natural does not matter. Sugar added by a cook counts as free sugar.

options.text: Only if it is white sugar.
options.feedback: Colour does not matter. Jaggery added to food counts like white sugar.

steps.takeaway: Added sugar, honey, syrup and juice count; whole fruit does not.

steps.title: The limit: under 10% of energy

hook.stem: On a 2,000 kcal day, how much free sugar fits under WHO's 10% limit?

options.feedback: Right. That is about 12 level teaspoons on a 2,000 kcal day.
That mixes up kcal and grams. 200 kcal of sugar is about 50 g.
That is far below the limit. 10% of 2,000 kcal is about 50 g.

steps.teach: WHO says free sugars should give under 10% of daily energy. On a 2,000 kcal day, that is about 50 g, or 12 teaspoons.

visual.label: Free sugar on a 2,000 kcal day

example.ask: Tap the comparison with the limit.
parts: Neha's sweet chai, biscuits and a cold drink
add up to about 60 g of free sugar,
which is more than the 50 g limit for her day.
example.spot: which is more than the 50 g limit for her day.
example.feedback: At about 60 g, she is past the 50 g that 10% of a 2,000 kcal day allows.

guided.stem: If 1 teaspoon holds about 4 g of sugar, how many teaspoons is 25 g?

options.feedback: Yes. 25 divided by 4 is about 6, the teaspoons WHO gives for 5%.
That counts grams, not teaspoons. Divide by 4 to get about 6.
That multiplies instead of dividing. 25 divided by 4 is about 6.

guided.stem: Why does 10% of 2,000 kcal come to about 50 g of sugar?
guided.hint: Each gram of sugar gives about 4 kcal.

options.text: 200 kcal at 4 kcal a gram is 50 g.
options.feedback: Right. 10% of 2,000 is 200 kcal, and 200 divided by 4 is 50 g.
10% of 2,000 is 200, in kcal. Dividing by 4 kcal a gram gives 50 g.
Sugar gives about 4 kcal for each gram, which is how kcal turn into grams.

steps.takeaway: Under 10% of energy: about 50 g on 2,000 kcal.

steps.title: Drinks hide a lot of sugar

hook.stem: Up to how much free sugar can one can of sweet soda hold?

options.feedback: Right. That is about 10 teaspoons in a single can.
That is closer to one spoon of ketchup. A can can hold up to 40 g.
It is mostly water, but a can can still hold up to 40 g of sugar.

steps.teach: Much sugar hides in drinks and packed foods. One can of sweet soda can hold up to 40 g. Even a spoon of ketchup has about 4 g.

example.ask: Tap where most of his sugar comes from.
parts: After cricket practice, Dev skips sweets all day
but drinks one can of cola,
and thinks he had almost no sugar.

guided.stem: A can holds 40 g of free sugar. What share of the 50 g limit is that?

options.feedback: Yes. 40 divided by 50 is 0.8, so one can uses about 80% of the limit.

The decimal slipped. 40 divided by 50 is 0.8, which is 80%.

guided.stem: Which of these hides free sugar that few people think of as sweet?
guided.hint: WHO gave a sauce as its example.

options.feedback: Right. One tablespoon of ketchup holds about 4 g of free sugar.
Plain rice has starch, not added sugar. Ketchup is the hidden source here.
Sugar inside fresh vegetables is not free sugar. Ketchup is the hidden one.

steps.takeaway: One can of soda can hold most of a day’s limit.

concepts.title: Hydration cues
concepts.hook: NHS counts tea and milk as fluid, calls its six-to-eight-cup figure a guide, and points to pee colour as a simple daily cue.
concepts.rule: Water, milk, tea and coffee all add fluid; about 6 to 8 cups a day is a guide. Pale yellow pee is the aim. Heat and long activity raise needs.

claims.text: NHS gives six to eight cups or glasses of fluid as a general guide, not a fixed water-only rule.
Water, lower-fat milk and lower-sugar drinks, including tea and coffee, all count towards daily fluid.
NHS says most people can aim for pee that is a clear pale yellow; dark yellow, strong-smelling pee is a sign of low fluid.
People may need more fluid in a hot place or when active for long periods, especially after sweating.
NHS suggests keeping fruit juice and smoothies to one small glass, 150 ml, a day.

items.stem: At school, Anu drinks no plain water but has 3 cups of milk and 2 cups of tea. By the NHS guide, how much fluid has she had?

options.feedback: Milk and tea both count towards daily fluid, so all 5 cups add up.
NHS counts milk, tea and coffee as fluid, not only plain water.
Tea counts as well, so her 2 cups of tea add to the total.

items.stem: A glass holds about 250 ml. Estimate the litres in the hydration guide's top figure of 8 glasses.

options.feedback: 8 glasses of 250 ml make 2,000 ml, which is 2 litres.
That counts each glass as a litre. Each one is a quarter litre.
The decimal slipped. 8 times 250 ml is 2,000 ml, or 2 litres.

items.stem: A poster says every person has to drink exactly 8 glasses of plain water a day. What is not quite right?

options.text: It is a 6 to 8 cup guide, and other drinks count.
options.feedback: NHS gives a range as a guide and counts milk, tea and coffee as well.

options.text: Nothing; 8 glasses of water is the rule.
options.feedback: NHS calls the figure a guide, and other drinks count towards it.

options.text: The guide is 15 glasses a day.
options.feedback: The NHS range is 6 to 8 cups or glasses, not 15.

items.stem: In the hostel after a long exam day with little to drink, Rohan notices dark, strong-smelling pee. What does the NHS link this to?

options.feedback: NHS lists dark yellow, strong-smelling pee as a cue of low fluid.
Plenty of water tends to give pale pee. Dark pee points the other way.
NHS links dark, strong-smelling pee with too little fluid.

items.stem: Which set of cues does the NHS list for when the body is short of fluid?

options.text: Thirst, a dry mouth and feeling tired.
options.feedback: All three are on the NHS list, along with dark pee and dizziness.

options.text: Pale pee and peeing more often.
options.feedback: Pale pee is the aim. The NHS cue is peeing less often than usual.
Neither is on the NHS list. Thirst, a dry mouth and tiredness are.

items.stem: A friend asks why families keep a closer eye on small children and grandparents on hot days. Which reply explains it best?

options.text: Babies, children and older adults are more at risk of low fluid.
options.feedback: NHS names babies, children and older adults as more at risk of dehydration.

options.text: They never sweat, so heat cannot affect them.
options.feedback: Heat affects every age. NHS says these groups are more at risk, not less.

options.text: Only athletes can run short of fluid.
options.feedback: Anyone can run short. NHS names the very young and the old as more at risk.

items.stem: Why do people need more fluid after long sport in the heat?

options.text: Sweat takes extra water out of the body.
options.feedback: NHS says to drink extra after sweating, since sweat carries water away.

options.text: Heat makes the body store more water.
options.feedback: Heat makes the body sweat, which takes water out rather than storing it.
Water is not made into muscle. It leaves the body as sweat.

items.stem: The NHS suggests keeping fruit juice and smoothies to one small glass of ___ a day.

options.feedback: NHS gives one small glass of 150 ml as the most for juice and smoothies combined.
That is more than three times the NHS figure of 150 ml.
NHS keeps juice and smoothies far lower, at one small 150 ml glass.

misconceptions.name: Only plain water counts
misconceptions.correction: Milk, tea and coffee add fluid too.

misconceptions.name: Eight glasses fits everyone
misconceptions.correction: The NHS figure is a guide that changes with conditions.

misconceptions.name: Heat does not change needs
misconceptions.correction: Hot places and long activity can raise fluid needs.

steps.title: Pee colour is a simple cue

That is darker still. The NHS aim is a clear pale yellow.

marks.text: Dark yellow: a cue for fluid

Pale yellow is the aim, not a cue of low fluid.

concepts.title: Sleep and recovery
concepts.hook: Sleep is active: the brain cycles through stages while the body carries out repair.
concepts.rule: Adults aged 18 to 60 need seven or more hours of sleep. Sleep runs in cycles of about 90 minutes, with more deep sleep early in the night. Steady habits help.

claims.text: CDC recommends seven or more hours of sleep for adults aged 18–60.
NIH says deep sleep comes in longer stretches in the first half of the night, and REM sleep starts about 90 minutes after falling asleep.
One full sleep cycle takes about 80 to 100 minutes, and most people go through four to six cycles a night.
CDC lists habits that help sleep: the same bed and wake time each day, devices off 30 minutes before bed, and no caffeine late in the day.
NIH notes that caffeine can take 8 hours or more to wear off fully.
CDC gives teens aged 13 to 17 a range of 8 to 10 hours of sleep.

options.text: The brain stays busy; in REM it is nearly as active as awake.

Sleep has busy stages. In REM, the brain is nearly as active as awake.

options.text: The brain is busy only in deep sleep.
options.feedback: REM sleep is when the brain is most active, nearly as active as awake.

items.stem: Put the start of a night of sleep in order.

options.feedback: Sleep begins in the light stages before it gets deeper.
Deep sleep comes in longer stretches early in the night.

items.stem: Riya's train leaves early, so she sleeps at 11 pm and wakes at 4:30 am. About how many 90-minute cycles fit in?

options.text: Caffeine can take 8 hours or more to wear off.

items.stem: Which bedroom does the CDC describe as good for sleep?

options.feedback: CDC lists a quiet, relaxing bedroom at a cool temperature.

misconceptions.name: Sleep is a blank state
misconceptions.correction: Sleep has stages. They repeat, and the brain acts in new ways in each stage.

misconceptions.name: One short night defines a person
misconceptions.correction: The adult guidance is a population guide, not a verdict on one night.

misconceptions.name: Late caffeine does not matter
misconceptions.correction: Caffeine can take 8 hours or more to wear off.

concepts.hook: A juice 'detox' promises 5 kg off in a week. India's food guide calls about half a kilo a week safe, and says no single food covers every need.
